assessments.title: Fast Hash Function (SHA-256) Inappropriately Used for Password Storage
assessments.confidence_rationale: Base 2.5 (static); adjustments: +0.2 known family, +0.2 explicit key/curve, +0.1 explicit usage -> final 3.00 (HIGH)
assessments.rationale: SHA-256 is an unkeyed general-purpose cryptographic hash function engineered for rapid computation. It lacks memory-hardness and work factor controls, enabling adversaries to execute billions of guesses per second on consumer GPUs.
assessments.quantum_relevance: Conventional security vulnerability, NOT a quantum risk. Grover's algorithm is irrelevant; classical offline cracking tools (hashcat, John the Ripper) break unsalted or fast hashes effortlessly today.

threat_analysis.details: Static security rule: Fast Hash Function (SHA-256) Inappropriately Used for Password Storage.

recommendation.action: Replace SHA-256 password storage immediately with a standardized, memory-hard password-hashing function such as Argon2id, bcrypt, or scrypt.
recommendation.reason: Password storage requires computational and memory hardness to defend against offline GPU/ASIC brute-force dictionary attacks. Post-quantum algorithms do not solve this problem.

assessments.title: Cryptographically Broken Hash Function MD5 in Active Use
assessments.confidence_rationale: Base 2.5 (static); adjustments: +0.2 known family, +0.1 explicit usage -> final 2.80 (HIGH)
assessments.rationale: MD5 suffers from catastrophic collision vulnerabilities, allowing practical chosen-prefix collision attacks in seconds on commodity hardware.
assessments.quantum_relevance: Classical cryptanalytic failure, not a quantum issue. MD5 was broken classically in 2004.

threat_analysis.details: Static security rule: Cryptographically Broken Hash Function MD5 in Active Use.

recommendation.action: Migrate from MD5 to SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-3 for integrity checks and signatures.
recommendation.reason: MD5 provides zero collision resistance. Attackers can forge valid certificates, signatures, or checksums.

assessments.title: Insecure Electronic Codebook (ECB) Cipher Mode
assessments.confidence_rationale: Base 2.5 (static); adjustments: +0.2 known family, +0.2 explicit key/curve, +0.1 explicit usage -> final 3.00 (HIGH)
assessments.rationale: Electronic Codebook (ECB) mode encrypts identical plaintext blocks into identical ciphertext blocks, preserving structural patterns and failing semantic security.
assessments.quantum_relevance: Mode of operation architectural failure, not a quantum issue.

threat_analysis.details: Static security rule: Insecure Electronic Codebook (ECB) Cipher Mode.

recommendation.action: Switch from ECB mode to an Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) mode such as GCM or CCM.
recommendation.reason: ECB mode leaks data confidentiality through structural pattern visibility and provides no message integrity.

assessments.title: Deprecated and Collision-Vulnerable Hash Function SHA-1 in Use
assessments.confidence_rationale: Base 2.5 (static); adjustments: +0.2 known family, +0.1 explicit usage -> final 2.80 (HIGH)
assessments.rationale: SHA-1 has practical collision vulnerabilities (SHAttered, Shambles attacks) and has been formally deprecated by NIST (NIST SP 800-131A) and major web browsers.
assessments.quantum_relevance: Classical collision vulnerability. This is a conventional hygiene issue, not a post-quantum migration issue.

threat_analysis.details: Static security rule: Deprecated and Collision-Vulnerable Hash Function SHA-1 in Use.

recommendation.action: Replace SHA-1 with modern hash algorithms such as SHA-256 or SHA-3.
recommendation.reason: SHA-1 collisions allow attackers to produce colliding documents or certificates with identical signatures.

assessments.title: RSA Digital Signature Vulnerable to Shor's Algorithm
assessments.confidence_rationale: Base 2.5 (static); adjustments: +0.2 known family, +0.2 explicit key/curve, +0.1 explicit usage -> final 3.00 (HIGH)
assessments.rationale: Shor's algorithm computes integer prime factors in polynomial time on a Cryptanalytically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC), breaking the mathematical assumption underlying RSA signature authenticity.
assessments.quantum_relevance: Directly vulnerable to polynomial-time forgery via Shor's algorithm once a CRQC is realized.

threat_analysis.details: Trust validity T (5.0y) + Migration Y (3.0y) = 8.0y is within CRQC Z (15.0y). Scheduled quantum migration recommended.

recommendation.action: Initiate quantum migration planning to transition public-key digital signatures to NIST-standardized Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) signature algorithms.
recommendation.reason: RSA signatures cannot withstand quantum cryptanalysis. Systems must migrate before long-lived certificates, trust anchors, or signed binaries outlive the CRQC horizon.

assessments.title: ECDSA Signature Vulnerable to Shor's Algorithm
assessments.confidence_rationale: Base 2.5 (static); adjustments: +0.2 known family, +0.2 explicit key/curve, +0.1 explicit usage -> final 3.00 (HIGH)
assessments.rationale: Shor's algorithm solves elliptic-curve discrete logarithms in polynomial time, completely compromising ECDSA private keys and enabling signature forgery.
assessments.quantum_relevance: Directly vulnerable via Shor's algorithm. All standard curves (NIST P-256, P-384, secp256k1) are broken.

threat_analysis.details: Trust validity T (5.0y) + Migration Y (3.0y) = 8.0y is within CRQC Z (15.0y). Scheduled quantum migration recommended.

recommendation.action: Transition to post-quantum signature schemes (NIST FIPS 204 ML-DSA or FIPS 205 SLH-DSA) or hybrid classical-quantum signatures.
recommendation.reason: ECDSA provides zero security against quantum adversaries capable of running Shor's algorithm.

assessments.title: AES-128 Effective Security Halved by Grover's Algorithm
assessments.confidence_rationale: Base 2.5 (static); adjustments: +0.2 known family, +0.2 explicit key/curve, +0.1 explicit usage -> final 3.00 (HIGH)
assessments.rationale: Grover's search algorithm provides a quadratic speedup for brute-force key search, reducing the effective security of AES-128 from 128 bits to approximately 64 bits.
assessments.quantum_relevance: Grover's algorithm provides a square-root speedup ($O(\sqrt{N})$), making 128-bit symmetric keys borderline for ultra-high-assurance or classified workloads.

threat_analysis.details: Grover's algorithm reduces 128-bit symmetric key to 64-bit effective quantum security. Insufficient for classified or multi-decade confidentiality.

recommendation.action: Upgrade symmetric encryption from AES-128 to AES-256 for long-term confidentiality.
recommendation.reason: AES-256 maintains a comfortable 128-bit quantum security margin against Grover's algorithm, satisfying post-quantum security requirements (e.g., NSA CNSA 2.0).
